newsitem.title: UK: Bankers say euro reserve rules could damage market.
newsitem.headline: Bankers say euro reserve rules could damage market.

text.p: Plans for reserve requirements under a future European Central Bank (ECB) are misguided and would drive business away from Europe, senior bankers said on Friday.
"In an open market, it (a reserve requirement) will...siphon banking business out of the euro area," said Tim Sweeney, director general of the British Banking Association (BBA).
Reserve requirements are the percentage of bank deposits that firms must set aside with their central bank. Lowering or raising this requirement effectively influences money supply.
European bankers slammed the European Monetary Institute (EMI) for leaving the door open to such requirements, which the Bank of England said would amount to a tax on the sector.
"The imposition of reserve requirements is unnecessary for the efficient conduct of monetary policy and threatens to distort the market," Sweeney said.

The BBA, which represents more than 300 British and overseas banks active in Britain, along with European counterparts such as Belgium and Luxembourg, expressed disappointment that the EMI was still looking at the possibility of minimum reserves.
While Sweeney said such a move would also lead to business moving away from the area covered by the euro, his Luxembourg counterpart Lucien Thiel said it may lead to a two-tier system.

"If (the ECB) insists on minimum reserves within the euro zone that don't pay interest, and the City of London does not have minimum reserves -- or does and pays interest -- London will become an offshore euro centre," Thiel said.
According to the association that represents private sector banks in Germany, where a reserve requirement is currently in force, the mechanism would be "superfluous."
The German bankers also said it would be harmful to financial centres in the future euro currency area and would make it harder for the ECB to conduct monetary policy.

Other industry associations expressed similar views. The French banking association suggested if requirements were imposed, they should bear interest. And the Bank of England (BoE) argued against reserve requirements on the basis that they imposed a tax on the institutions covered by them.
The BoE also said reserve requirements were inferior to market approaches, which could be used for the same ends.

But the French, believed to be keen on the idea of using minimum reserves to control money market volatility, argue that without them, an ECB would be obliged to conduct daily "fine tuning" operations of the type currently carried out by the BoE to smooth volatility in money market rates.
The EMI, which said earlier that final decisions on several key issues would have to be made by the ECB, did not specify which firms would be subject to a reserve.
It said only that in considering the efficiency of a such a system, the ECB "might need to impose reserve ratios on a broad range of liabilities and institutions".

It said it needed to study further the extension of the definition in the relevant article "so as to allow the ECB to subject a broader range of financial institutions than credit institutions alone to reserve requirements".
The terms and conditions of any such system would be uniform throughout the area covered by a single currency, it said.
The ECB, which will take over monetary policy responsibility as soon as the European single currency is launched in 1999, will not be up and running until 1998.
